item.title: Foldable Phones and Accessibility: Benefits, Barriers, Weight, Care, and Cost
item.content:encoded:
![Smiling woman interacting with foldable phone](https://assets.buttondown.email/images/fa2b0717-274d-478c-a011-c39fb95e727c.jpeg?w=960&fit=max)
*Smiling woman interacting with foldable phone*
Apple announced the iPhone Duo, its first foldable iPhone, on September 9, 2026. [ABC News reported](https://abcnews.com/Business/apple-set-announce-new-products/story?id=136299541&utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits) a starting price of $1,999, with the phone arriving in stores on October 23. With Apple joining Samsung, Google, and Motorola, foldable phones are getting more attention this fall than they have since the category launched in 2018.
Accessibility professionals will get questions from clients, colleagues, and disabled friends and family about whether these phones are a good choice for a particular person.
# Where Foldables Help
**A larger screen that still fits in a pocket**: Book-style foldables open to an inner display of about 7.6 to 8 inches. The iPhone Duo and the Galaxy Z Fold8 open to 7.6 inches, and the [Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra](https://www.samsung.com/us/smartphones/galaxy-z-fold8-ultra/?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits) opens to 8 inches. For people with low vision who use screen magnification or very large text, a wider screen means less horizontal panning and more words visible at the same zoom level. Text that wraps into a narrow column on a standard phone can display in longer lines.
**Hands-free positions:** Foldable phones can stand on their own when partially folded. Samsung calls this Flex Mode, and Apple says the [iPhone Duo can be used partially folded](https://abcnews.com/Business/apple-set-announce-new-products/story?id=136299541&utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits). A phone that holds itself up is useful for several groups:
- Deaf and hard of hearing people who sign on video calls, since signing needs both hands free and the camera at a steady angle.
- People with tremor, weak grip, or fatigue who find it hard to hold a phone through a long call or video.
- People who need to follow captions or instructions while their hands are occupied with something else
**More room for AAC and multitasking:** Many people who use augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) apps carry a tablet because a standard phone screen cannot show enough symbols at a usable size. An open foldable offers a larger grid in a device that closes to pocket size. Split-screen use can also help, for example, keeping a live transcription app on one half of the screen while a meeting or document is open on the other half.
**A cover screen for quick tasks:** The outer screen handles short tasks such as reading a notification or sending a quick reply without opening the phone. For someone who finds unfolding difficult, a capable cover screen reduces how often they have to do it. According to [T-Mobile's lineup overview](https://www.t-mobile.com/dialed-in/devices/samsung-foldable-phone-zfold8-zflip8-zfold8-ultra?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits), the Galaxy Z Fold8 has a 5.5-inch cover screen, and the Galaxy Z Flip8 has a 4.1-inch cover screen.
# Where Foldables Create Barriers
**Barrier 1: Folding and unfolding requires manual dexterity that many people do not have:** Opening and closing a foldable is a two-handed (or hand substitute) task for most users. It requires a combination of physical abilities:
- Enough grip strength to hold one half of the phone steady
- Enough pinch or push strength to overcome the hinge resistance and the magnets that hold the phone closed
- Enough coordination between both hands to do this without dropping the phone
Many disabled people do not have that combination. This includes people with arthritis, cerebral palsy, Parkinson’s disease or essential tremor, multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injuries that affect hand function, Stroke, particularly with weakness on one side of the body, and limb differences.
Some clamshell flip phones can be opened with one thumb, but that takes controlled force applied at the edge of the phone, which is the same kind of fine motor movement that is hard for people with tremor or weak fingers. When a phone’s best features sit behind a physical fold, a person who cannot open it is left with the cover screen, a smaller, more cramped experience than a standard phone at a fraction of the price. Opening force also isn't a standard item on manufacturer spec sheets, so buyers have no way to compare hinges before trying one in a store.
**Barrier 2: Layout changes at different breakpoints:** Websites and apps switch between layouts at set screen widths called breakpoints. On a standard phone, people rarely cross a breakpoint in the middle of a task. On a foldable, every fold or unfold can cross one, and foldables produce screen widths that many sites and apps have never been tested at, including:
- The cover screen
- The inner screen, which is close to square on newer book-style models
- Each half of a split-screen view, which can be about as narrow as a standard phone
When a site or app crosses a breakpoint, navigation and content can move to different places on the screen, and screen reader and switch users have to relearn where things are. If the new layout presents content or focus in an order that does not make sense, it can fail [WCAG Success Criterion 1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/meaningful-sequence.html?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits) or [Success Criterion 2.4.3 Focus Order](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/focus-order.html?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits). At 200 percent zoom on the inner screen, a low vision user can end up with the mobile layout on a device the site treats as a tablet, so testing needs to cover each screen at more than one zoom level. Google's [window size classes](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/layouts/adaptive/window-size-classes?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits) give Android app teams a defined set of widths to test against.
**Barrier 3: One-handed and left-handed use:** Researchers presenting at CHI 2026 found that one-handed use of an open foldable with content on both halves [requires users to change their grip to reach each screen](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3772318.3790528?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits). On book-style foldables, the hinge sits on the left edge, which [pushes the power button and fingerprint sensor to the right side](https://www.androidpolice.com/good-folding-phone-lefties-doesnt-exist/?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits) on many models. A person who only uses their left hand may find unlocking the phone and reaching controls harder than on a standard phone.
**Barrier 4: Screen changes when the phone folds or unfolds**: When a user opens or closes a foldable, the app on screen has to redraw for a different size and shape. Apps that do not handle this change reload the page, lose what the user typed into a form, or send screen reader focus back to the top of the screen. For a blind user, losing focus halfway through a form means finding their place again one element at a time, which can take minutes. The problem comes from how the app is built, and many apps have not yet been updated to handle fold changes.
**Barrier 5: The fold:** Visibility of items crossing through the fold crease has improved, and [T-Mobile describes the Galaxy Z Fold8](https://www.t-mobile.com/cell-phone/samsung-galaxy-z-fold8?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits) as near crease-free. A visible crease can still distort text and images running across the middle of the screen, which is more noticeable at high magnification. A crease that can be felt can also interfere with swipe gestures and small touch targets near the fold.
**Barrier 6: Weight:** Weight matters for people with arthritis, muscle weakness, chronic pain, or fatigue-related conditions, and for anyone who holds a phone for long stretches. Foldables are no longer dramatically heavier than large standard phones, but weights vary a lot from model to model.

Sources: [T-Mobile](https://www.t-mobile.com/dialed-in/devices/samsung-foldable-phone-zfold8-zflip8-zfold8-ultra?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits), [Samsung](https://www.samsung.com/us/smartphones/galaxy-z-fold8-ultra/?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits), [PhoneArena](https://www.phonearena.com/news/pixel-11-pro-fold-is-here_id182546?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits), [Android Central](https://www.androidcentral.com/phones/google-pixel-11-pro-fold?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits), [MacObserver](https://www.macobserver.com/tips/round-ups/iphone-duo-design-5-2-mm-grade-5-titanium-ceramic-shield-ip68/?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits), [ABC News](https://abcnews.com/Business/apple-set-announce-new-products/story?id=136299541&utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits), [AT&T](https://www.att.com/buy/phones/samsung-galaxy-z-fold8.html?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits), [CNET via Yahoo Tech](https://tech.yahoo.com/phones/articles/galaxy-z-flip-8-vs-153053400.html?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits), and [Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/best-foldable-phones-2026/?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits). Prices are U.S. starting list prices before trade-ins, carrier credits, or sales.
For comparison, the non-folding [iPhone 18 Pro weighs 211 grams](https://www.macobserver.com/tips/round-ups/iphone-18-pro-vs-iphone-duo-weight-size-211-g-vs-254-g-pocket/?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits) and the [iPhone 18 Pro Max weighs 249 grams](https://www.macrumors.com/2026/09/09/iphone-duo-thinnest-iphone/?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits). The Galaxy Z Flip8 is lighter than both, while the iPhone Duo is Apple’s heaviest iPhone to date.
An open book-style foldable is roughly twice as wide as it is closed, so holding it in one hand puts the weight farther from the wrist. Reviewers have noted that [the weight difference becomes obvious when you hold an unfolded phone in one hand](https://www.androidheadlines.com/2026/09/iphone-duo-is-thicker-heavier-than-every-direct-competitor-that-could-be-a-problem.html?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits). The added leverage makes an open foldable feel heavier and demands more grip strength than its grams suggest. A protective case adds more weight and thickness, and a bulky case can also make the phone harder to open.
**Barrier 7: Special Care and Handling:** Foldables need more careful handling than standard phones. [Samsung's precautions for its foldable devices](https://www.samsung.com/uk/support/mobile-devices/precautions-when-using-the-galaxy-foldable-devices/?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits) include the following:
- Do not press the main screen with a hard or sharp object, such as a pen or a fingernail, and do not apply excessive pressure
- Do not remove the preinstalled screen protector film, and do not add other films or stickers
- Do not leave cards, coins, or keys between the screens when folding the phone
- Fold the phone before putting it away, and do not store it open
- Keep the phone a safe distance from credit cards and implantable medical devices because of the magnets inside, and consult a physician before use if you have an implanted medical device
Several of these rules conflict with the way many disabled people use their phones. People who cannot use a fingertip often touch the screen with a knuckle, a fingernail, a stylus, a mouth stick, or a head pointer. Many adaptive styluses have hard tips. Samsung warns that hard or sharp objects on the inner screen can scratch or damage the display. Confirm that a specific stylus or pointer is safe for the inner screen before using it.
Because owners are told not to remove the factory screen protector on the inner screen, Samsung has directed owners to [an authorized service center for replacement](https://www.samsung.com/ca/support/mobile-devices/galaxy-z-fold2-care/?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits). Getting to a service center is a significant barrier for someone who depends on paratransit or lives far from one, and mail-in service can leave them without a phone for days.
**Barrier 8: Magnets and implanted medical devices**: Foldables contain magnets that help hold them closed and align them on wireless chargers. People with pacemakers, implanted defibrillators, or other implanted medical devices such as cochlear implants should talk with their physician before using a foldable phone.
**Barrier 9: Dust, sand, and water**: Dust and water protection differs across models. The 2026 Samsung foldables are rated IP48, and an IP4X rating [protects against solid objects larger than 1 mm but is not fully dust-tight](https://www.phonearena.com/news/pixel-10-pro-fold-is-it-dust-water-resistant_id173371?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits). The Pixel 11 Pro Fold and iPhone Duo carry IP68 ratings. Fine grit in a hinge can cause damage over time, which is worth considering for anyone whose phone rides in a bag or mount on a mobility aid that goes outdoors.
**Barrier 10: Drops and repair costs:** People with tremor, weak grip, or reduced sensation in their hands are more likely to drop a phone. Inner screen repairs on foldables are expensive, and some manufacturer repair programs specifically exclude them. Google’s store notes that its [$0 screen repair offer does not cover the inner screens of Pixel Fold phones](https://store.google.com/category/phones?hl=en-US&utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits). Anyone considering a foldable should add the cost of insurance or a protection plan to the purchase price.
**Barrier 11: Mounts and holders**: Wheelchair mounts, bed mounts, and AAC mounts are generally sized for standard phones. The [iPhone Duo is 11.3 mm thick when closed, compared with 8.75 mm for the iPhone 18 Pro](https://www.macobserver.com/tips/round-ups/iphone-18-pro-vs-iphone-duo-weight-size-211-g-vs-254-g-pocket/?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits), and it is [164.6 mm wide when open](https://www.pcguide.com/smartphone/iphone-18-pro-pro-max-and-iphone-duo-dimensions-weight-explained/?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits). Before buying, confirm that an existing mount can hold the phone in the position the user actually needs, and that the clamps do not press on the hinge or the inner screen.
# Price Is the Biggest Barrier
For many disabled people, and particularly for those who rely on disability benefits, a foldable is cost-prohibitive.
**Disabled people are far more likely to live in poverty:** According to the [2026 Annual Disability Statistics Compendium](https://www.researchondisability.org/resource/2026-disability-statistics-compendium-adsc/section-6-poverty-compendium-2026?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits), which uses American Community Survey data, 23.6 percent of people with disabilities ages 18 to 64 living in the community were in poverty in 2024, compared with 9.6 percent of people without disabilities. Smartphone ownership also differs by disability status. In a [Pew Research Center survey](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2021/09/10/americans-with-disabilities-less-likely-than-those-without-to-own-some-digital-devices/?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits), 72 percent of adults with a disability owned a smartphone, compared with 88 percent of adults without a disability.
**SSI payment and resource limits:** The [maximum federal Supplemental Security Income (SSI) payment for 2026](https://www.ssa.gov/ssi/amount?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits) is $994 per month for an individual. The least expensive iPhone Duo costs more than two full months of the maximum federal SSI payment, before sales tax, a case, or a protection plan. The cheapest current flip phone, the [Motorola Razr (2026), starts at $800](https://tech.yahoo.com/phones/articles/galaxy-z-flip-8-vs-153053400.html?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits), which is still most of a month's maximum federal SSI payment.
SSI also limits [countable resources to $2,000 for an individual](https://www.ssa.gov/ssi/text-resources-ussi.htm?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits). Household goods and personal effects don't count, so the phone itself doesn’t count once it’s been purchased. Saving close to $2,000 in cash to buy one leaves almost no room under the limit, and any other savings would push the person over it and put their benefits at risk. ABLE accounts can help some people save without that problem, but eligibility rules apply, and many people don't know these accounts exist or that they don’t have access to them.
**Carrier deals:** Advertised deals that bring a foldable close to free usually come with conditions. [AT&T's Galaxy Z Fold8 offer](https://www.att.com/buy/phones/samsung-galaxy-z-fold8.html?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits) requires a trade-in worth $290 or more and a qualifying unlimited plan, with the savings delivered as bill credits over time. [T-Mobile's financing terms](https://www.t-mobile.com/cell-phone/samsung-galaxy-z-fold8?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits) are limited to well-qualified buyers. Someone with an older phone, a prepaid plan, or a limited credit history will usually pay much closer to full price.
**Fewer lower-cost options**: Samsung released a lower-priced Galaxy Z Flip7 FE in 2025, but [it did not get a successor in 2026](https://www.phonearena.com/news/samsung-galaxy-z-fold-8-z-flip-8-expensive-could-have-been-much-worse-editorial_id181679?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits). That leaves the Motorola Razr as the main foldable option under $1,000 in the U.S. A large standard phone paired with an inexpensive stand delivers several of the same benefits described earlier at a much lower cost.
# Recommendations for disabled buyers and the people who advise them
- Try the exact model in a store, and open and close it several times with your own hands before buying
- Test the phone with your screen reader, magnification, switch access, or voice control turned on
- Start filling out a form in an app you use often, then fold and unfold the phone to see whether you lose your place
- Check whether your stylus, case, and mount work with the phone in both the folded and unfolded positions
- Find out the return window before you buy, and include a protection plan in the total cost
- Compare the total cost against a large standard phone plus a stand
### For app and website teams, including public entities
- Test on at least one book-style foldable and one flip-style foldable
- Make sure content reflows at both the cover screen and inner screen sizes without horizontal scrolling, consistent with [WCAG Success Criterion 1.4.10 Reflow](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/reflow.html?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits)
- Do not lock content to a single display orientation, consistent with [WCAG Success Criterion 1.3.4 Orientation](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/orientation.html?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits)
- Preserve form data, scroll position, and screen reader focus when the fold state changes
- Do not make any feature depend on the phone being folded or unfolded
State and local governments covered by the Department of Justice's [Title II web content and mobile app accessibility rule](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-28/chapter-I/part-35/subpart-H?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits) must meet [WCAG 2.1 Level AA](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/?utm_source=access-ability&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=foldable-phones-and-accessibility-benefits). A city or county app that loses a resident’s data or fails to reflow when the phone is unfolded can fail WCAG 2.1 success criteria and create compliance exposure under that rule.
## For manufacturers
- Publish hinge opening force in product specifications so buyers can compare models
- Offer lower-cost foldable models
- Provide care and handling instructions in accessible formats, in addition to setup screens and printed inserts
- Design button and fingerprint sensor placement that works for left-handed and one-handed users
- Include inner screens in screen repair programs
item.dc:creator: Access * Ability

item.title: Table or List? Choosing the Right Structure for Accessible Content
item.description: Tables and lists are both very useful ways to organize and present content. But they’re both structured to present different types of content. Choosing the right one isn't just a design decision.
item.content:encoded:
Tables and lists are both very useful ways to organize and present content. But they’re both structured to present different types of content. Choosing the right one isn't just a design decision. It’s also an editorial and accessibility decision. The right choice can make content easier to understand and navigate for everyone, including people who use screen readers, magnification, keyboard navigation, or mobile devices.
**Let’s start with a question**: Is the content relational data, or is it simply a group of related items?
**Answer**: If rows and columns are needed to make sense of the relationship between data points, use a table. If not, consider using a list.
For example, a class schedule.
A simple list would tell you that Biology meets on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. But with the row-and-column relationship, you can quickly associate a particular course with a particular day and time.
**Course**
**Monday**
**Wednesday**
**Friday**
Biology 101
9:00 AM
9:00 AM
9:00 AM
English 201
10:30 AM
No class
10:30 AM
Chemistry 110
No class
1:00 PM
No class
## When Should You Use a List?
Use a list when you're presenting a collection of related items, concepts, or steps.
Lists work particularly well for:
- Steps in a process or procedure. - A collection of related items. - Requirements or recommendations.
Lists are generally easy to scan visually, straightforward for screen reader users to navigate, and require less cognitive effort, making information easier to understand quickly.
They are especially helpful on smaller screens because list items reflow naturally to the available space rather than requiring horizontal scrolling.
**Note:** As [Dax Castro](https://www.linkedin.com/in/daxcastro/ "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") points out, [long,nested lists](https://lnkd.in/p/eUNEnxzx "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") can overwhelm screen reader users and folks with cognitive challenges. So keep your lists simple, no more than two levels deep.
### Make Your List Accessible
Instead of creating the appearance of a list with manually typed bullet symbols or numbers, use proper semantic HTML with **<ul>** for unordered lists and **<ol>** for ordered, sequential step lists.
This supports [WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.1, Info and Relationships](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/info-and-relationships "This link leaves the DubBlog website."), which requires meaningful structure and relationships to be programmatically determinable.
Use **bulleted lists** for a list of related items. For example:
- Apples - Oranges - Bananas - Grapes - Strawberries
Use a **numbered list** when order matters, such as steps that must be completed in a specific sequence. For example:
1. Open the website. 2. Select Sign In. 3. Enter your username and password. 4. Select Submit. 5. Confirm that you’re signed in.
## When Should You Use a Table?
Use a table when people need to understand relationships between two data points. For example, the class schedule above, financial data, statistics, or other content where the meaning of the data in one cell depends on its corresponding row and column headers.
For example, this high tide schedule.
For this type of content, a table is more effective than a list because the information has multiple related attributes of _Day, Time,_ and _Tide Level_ that need to be compared across rows to make sense and be of value.
**Day**
**Time**
**Tide Level**
Monday
8:15 AM
3.2 ft
Tuesday
9:02 AM
3.5 ft
Wednesday
9:48 AM
3.7 ft
Using a table to convey this type of content helps:
- make relationships clear, as each day is directly associated with its corresponding time and tide level. - support quick comparisons so the reader can scan down the columns to compare times or tide levels across days. - provide a consistent structure with each row following the same pattern, making the information predictable and easier to understand.
Tables can be particularly useful for people who need to compare multiple pieces of content at once. But they can also be harder to navigate with a screen reader or on a small screen, so they shouldn't be the default choice when a list or even a paragraph would communicate the information just as well.
When in doubt as to whether to use a table or a list, go back to our original question (and the answer) at the beginning of this blog post:
**Is the content relational data, or is it simply a group of related items?**
### Make Your Table Accessible
- Use [proper semantic table markup](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/table "This link leaves the DubBlog website."), not a visual grid. - Identify row and column headers with **<th>**. - Associate headers and data cells so meaning is programmatically determined. - Provide a [meaningful caption](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/caption "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") when useful. - Keep the structure simple and avoid merged cells. - Ensure sufficient [text and background contrast](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/contrast-minimum.html "This link leaves the DubBlog website.").
These practices also support [WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.1, Info and Relationships](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/info-and-relationships "This link leaves the DubBlog website."), by ensuring that relationships between headers and data can be programmatically determined.
## Simplicity is an Accessibility Strategy
Accessibility isn’t always about technology. Sometimes, it’s about the content itself and making thoughtful, strategic choices about how that content is structured from the start. The goal is to choose the simplest structure that communicates information clearly and works well for the widest range of people. Knowing when to use a table and when a simple list will do is an editorial and design decision that will make content easier to scan, understand, and navigate.
Good accessibility often starts with simple choices like less complexity, more clarity, and a structure that helps people get to the information they need.
## Resources
- [7 Core Accessibility Skills > Lists](https://accessibility.umn.edu/guides-resources/7-core-accessibility-skills/lists "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") - [When to use tables: Ensuring accessibility for all](https://www.digital.nsw.gov.au/article/when-to-use-tables-ensuring-accessibility-for-all "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") - [Avoid Excessive Bullet Levels](https://lnkd.in/p/eUNEnxzx "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") (LinkedIn, [Dax Castro](https://www.linkedin.com/in/daxcastro/ "This link leaves the DubBlog website.")) - [Accessibility tip: Sometimes a table isn't the best option](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/toddmarquisboutin_accessibility-education-edtech-activity-7376641001924218881-Lj5X?utm_source=share&utm_medium=member_desktop&rcm=ACoAAACmLHMBpb9Qho4Thxy4VJBQ9l5qz-BYvzA "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") (LinkedIn, [Todd Marquis Boutin](https://www.linkedin.com/in/toddmarquisboutin/ "This link leaves the DubBlog website."))

item.title: Understanding Accessibility Debt: How It Happens and What to Do About It
item.description: Folks rarely set out to build something inaccessible. But tight deadlines, understaffing, and budget constraints can push shift-left accessibility activities to the sidelines, creating gaps and
item.content:encoded:
Folks rarely set out to build something inaccessible. But tight deadlines, understaffing, and budget constraints can push [shift-left accessibility activities](https://www.lullabot.com/articles/what-it-means-shift-left-accessibility-and-how-do-it-right "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") to the sidelines, creating gaps and missteps that are harder to address later. Issues like a button without a label, an image missing ALT text, or an unlabeled form field. On their own, they sound minor, but left unresolved, they build up into a backlog. That backlog is called accessibility debt.
And that backlog can make it difficult, or even impossible, for many people to use your website, app, or software. Not to mention, the longer it goes ignored, the harder and [more costly it becomes to fix](../2024/want-to-save-money-make-your-website-accessible.html).
## How Does Accessibility Debt Happen?
Accessibility debt can build up in small ways:
- Moving files from concept to development without accounting for accessibility. - Reusing existing patterns and components to save time, without anyone evaluating their accessibility, can replicate the same accessibility issues from project to project. - Tight timelines can push testing to just mouse and keyboard, leaving other ways of interacting - screen readers, for example - out of the process. - A lack of accessibility training and expertise can make issues harder to spot.
Over time, these shortcuts add up, and what started as a few overlooked issues can become a much larger accessibility problem.
## Real-World Consequences
Accessibility debt isn't simply a backlog of technical issues. It's the accumulating cost of leaving them unresolved. The longer they remain, the more they can affect your users, designers and developers, budgets, timelines, and organizational risk. Accessibility debt has real operational consequences, such as:
- Loss of user trust. When prospective customers, students, employees, donors, or community members repeatedly encounter an inaccessible digital experience, they may stop relying on your website or choose another organization’s website that is easier to use, possibly causing you to lose revenue as well.
- Backlog becomes harder to prioritize. As the number of unresolved issues grows, it becomes harder to distinguish between quick wins, systemic problems, and issues that have the greatest impact on users.
- Support requests increase. People who can't complete tasks independently may need to contact support, request alternative formats, or ask someone else for help.
- Compliance and legal risk can increase. Constant accessibility issues can contribute to user complaints, investigations, or legal action, depending on the organization and applicable requirements.
- Time spent fixing the same issues repeatedly. Without addressing the underlying process or pattern, designers, developers, and content creators may keep encountering and repairing the same or similar accessibility issues.
- Remediation competes with new priorities. Accessibility fixes have to share limited time and resources with new features, redesigns, content initiatives, and other organizational priorities.
- Development and project schedules get disrupted. Last-minute accessibility fixes can force designers, developers, and content creators to revisit completed work, possibly delaying launches or releases.
- Accessibility work becomes harder to defend. If accessibility wasn't established [as part of the project requirements, standards, or the Definition of Done](accessibility-belongs-in-your-project-requirements.html), you may find yourself having to make a new case for why an issue needs to be fixed after the work was already considered completed.
The biggest consequence of accessibility debt is the people it leaves behind. People who can’t access information, complete a task, apply for something, make a purchase, register for an event, or participate because a digital barrier gets in their way. And often, the people most affected can’t even get far enough into the experience to report the problem. So, how do you determine your accessibility and start paying down that debt?
## How To Uncover and Start Eliminating Accessibility Debt
Accessibility debt won’t resolve itself. The first step is understanding where those barriers exist, then putting a plan in place to address them.
The first step is understanding the scope of the problem, and that starts with thorough testing. [Automated tools](automated-testing-is-a-rockstar-too.html) like DubBot can quickly flag common accessibility issues, and [manual testing](the-role-of-context-awareness-in-manual-accessibility-testing.html) like using keyboard navigation, screen readers, and focus-order checks helps uncover barriers automation can miss.
Next, track the problem like any other metric: open violations by severity, unaudited components, and meeting accessibility standards on every new feature, so you don't create new issues while fixing old ones. Prioritizing the most visible or disruptive barriers helps focus limited time and resources where they make the biggest difference, while also helping make the case for continued accessibility work. Read or listen to [_7 Core Accessibility Skills_](https://accessibility.umn.edu/guides-resources/7-core-accessibility-skills "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") from the University of Minnesota for information on high-impact, quick-win accessibility fixes.
Give the whole team, not just one specialist, [working knowledge of accessibility basics](https://www.w3.org/WAI/fundamentals/accessibility-intro/ "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") and remediation best practices. [Make training a regular, required activity](people-the-foundation-of-web-governance.html) for designers, developers, and content creators across your organization.
Build accessibility into design and code reviews, not a separate audit at the end. This is what shifting left in accessibility looks like. Make accessibility part of the project process from the very beginning. From project requirements to acceptance testing.
Review your content strategy and make sure you have included accessibility. [_True strategic planning integrates accessibility_](where-does-accessibility-fit-in-your-content-strategy.html) _alongside audience and persona research, positioning accessibility and inclusion as core business insights rather than afterthoughts._
Most importantly, [include people with disabilities in the testing process](https://www.w3.org/WAI/test-evaluate/involving-users/ "This link leaves the DubBlog website."). They’ll find what a checklist can’t. Automated and manual testing can tell you whether specific accessibility requirements are met. Still, people with disabilities can identify real-world usability issues and tell you whether a website actually works for them, where the experience breaks down, and why. Involving people with disabilities brings lived experience into the development process, with their feedback shaping design, content, functionality, and testing practices while helping identify and address accessibility issues before they become harder and more expensive to fix.
## Going From Accessibility Debt to Accessibility System
Think of [accessibility as a system](accessibility-is-a-system.html), not a one-time fix for accumulated debt. Fixing today’s issues is important, but it’s only part of the work. Lasting accessibility comes from building it into how your organization operates using [clear strategy](../2025/building-a-sustainable-web-accessibility-strategy.html), shared rules, defined ownership, and ongoing oversight. Strategy sets the direction. [Policy sets the expectations](../2025/accessibility-policy-what-it-is-and-why-you-need-one.html). [Continuous monitoring](../2025/a-guide-to-continuous-accessibility-monitoring.html) provides the ongoing feedback needed to identify new issues as your website changes. Together, they turn accessibility from a backlog to manage into an ongoing practice.
## Resources
- [What is Accessibility Debt](https://www.boia.org/blog/what-is-accessibility-debt "This link leaves the DubBlog website.")? - [Why Accessibility Is An Operational Capability, Not A Feature](https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2026/06/why-accessibility-operational-capability-not-feature/ "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") - [Accessibility Technical Debt: Why It Compounds and How to Fix It](https://testparty.ai/blog/accessibility-technical-debt-explained "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") - [Understanding Accessibility Debt: What It Is and How to Manage It](https://www.pivotalaccessibility.com/2024/10/understanding-accessibility-debt-what-it-is-and-how-to-manage-it/ "This link leaves the DubBlog website.")

item.title: Interview Accommodations: A Legal Necessity, not a Favor
item.description: When companies talk about diversity and inclusion, they often forget about a crucial aspect: accessibility in the hiring process.
item.content:encoded:
![Woman in wheelchair speaking with two other women in a business setting](https://assets.buttondown.email/images/f4544aab-f214-4105-beb3-ec0b4dbd4ada.jpeg?w=960&fit=max)
*Woman in wheelchair speaking with two other women in a business setting*
When companies talk about diversity and inclusion, they often forget about a crucial aspect: accessibility in the hiring process.
Did you know that your obligations as an employer under the EEOC begin with an employee’s candidacy?
Don’t you want your candidates to be able to show their best selves during the interview process?
If you want to build a truly inclusive team, your interviews must be accessible to everyone, including people with disabilities. Otherwise, you’re not just missing out on talent but actively discriminating against it.
Accommodations during interviews are essential, not special favors or extras. Just as you wouldn’t conduct an in-person interview without a chair for the candidate, you shouldn’t conduct one without considering what a candidate with a disability might need that you haven’t anticipated. Here are some critical and common accommodations that should be on every employer’s checklist.
## **1\. Sign Language Interpreter: More Than Just Hand Movements**
The EEOC loves to issue huge fines against companies that cancel interviews when the candidate requests an interpreter. Hiring a sign language interpreter isn’t just about communication; it’s about respecting the candidate’s language and culture. For Deaf candidates in the US, American Sign Language (ASL) is typically their primary language, though other sign languages include SEE, Cued Speech, and Tactile. Expecting Deaf candidates to lip-read or rely on written communication is like asking someone who speaks only Mandarin to interview in English.
When arranging for a sign language interpreter, ensure they are certified and experienced in ASL. Best practice is to get an interpreter who specializes in the vocabulary discussed in the interview, such as legal, medical, or engineering. This isn’t a job for your cousin who took a few sign language classes in college. Professional interpreters ensure nothing gets mixed up or confused and allow the candidates to fully express themselves and understand what’s being asked.
Book the interpreter well in advance. Last-minute scrambling is not an option. Ensure the interpreter has enough context about the interview to prepare appropriately. Also, remember that the interpreter is there to facilitate communication, not to participate in the interview. They should position themselves so the candidate can maintain eye contact with the interviewer, not the interpreter. The interviewer should speak with the candidate, not the interpreter.
## **2\. High-Quality Closed Captioning**
If you’re interviewing someone Deaf or hard of hearing, they might also request high-quality closed captioning or Communication Access Realtime Translation (CART). People with longstanding hearing loss who speak may have what’s called dysfluent speech, or colloquially, a “deaf accent,” which AI and automatic captioning struggle with. Don’t cheap out and rely on AI/auto-generated captions that might turn “I have experience in leadership roles” into “I have expertise in leaping trolls.” It’s not just frustrating; it’s unprofessional and can drastically change what you or the candidate are communicating.
CART services provide word-for-word transcription of spoken communication, delivered in real time. “Respeaking” is a lower-quality form of captioning that does not provide an equal experience. CART ensures accuracy where the candidate receives the same information as everyone else in the room. If your company doesn’t have a contract with a CART vendor, the time to fix that is before you need their services. This isn’t just about the interview; it’s about every stage of the hiring process, from phone screens to final rounds.
## **3\. Accessible Facility / Teleconference software**
Imagine being invited to an interview and discovering there’s nowhere to park. Once you get in, the conference room is stuffed with furniture that makes wheelchair navigation impossible. This isn’t just an inconvenience. Facilities must be accessible. Accessible parking must be close to the building’s entrance, with a clear path to the door and no obstructions like construction equipment or delivery trucks. The pathway to the interview area should be clear of obstacles, and the interviewer should be able to reach it easily.
If the interview is virtual, this might seem moot, but don’t forget that candidates with disabilities might still need to visit your office at some point. Also, consider your virtual interview tools. Ask the candidate for their preference, because some tools work better than others when used with assistive technology. Having an accessible interview environment isn’t just about complying with the ADA; it’s about showing that your company genuinely cares about all employees’ needs.
## **4\. Breaks and Extra Time**
Not every candidate can sit through a 90-minute intense interview without a break. Some people with disabilities, such as those with chronic pain or fatigue, may need to take short breaks to stretch, rest, or manage their symptoms. Neurodiverse people also often need a few minutes to mentally decompress and reset between interviewers. Denying this isn’t just inconsiderate; it can also mean missing out on a great candidate who needs a bit more flexibility.
When scheduling interviews, ask candidates if they need breaks or additional time. This can be especially important in interview scenarios where multiple tasks or questions are presented in a single session. For example, a candidate with a cognitive disability may need extra time to process questions and formulate responses. Accommodating these needs isn’t about giving someone an unfair advantage; it’s about leveling the playing field.
## **5\. Questions in Advance**
For candidates with disabilities, especially those with cognitive or anxiety-related conditions, getting questions in advance can be the difference between a successful interview and a disaster. Some disabilities affect processing speed or the ability to think on the spot, making traditional interview formats challenging.
Providing questions in advance lets candidates prepare thoughtful, thorough responses that reflect their abilities. This practice benefits all candidates, not just those with disabilities. It also improves the likelihood that all candidates are asked the same questions, which should help eliminate bias.
## **6\. Alternative Test Formats**
Some roles require candidates to complete tests or assessments during the interview process. For candidates with disabilities, the standard test format might not be accessible or might not accurately measure their abilities. For example, a timed written test might disadvantage someone with a learning disability or physical impairment that affects writing speed.
Offering alternative test formats is crucial. This might mean providing extra time, allowing assistive technology, or offering a different type of assessment altogether, such as a verbal explanation instead of a written one. The key is to focus on the skill you are assessing, not the mechanism used to assess it. If the goal is to evaluate knowledge, does it matter if the solution is typed, spoken, or drawn?
## **The Bottom Line: Timely Accessibility Is Non-Negotiable**
If your interview process isn’t accessible, you’re not just failing people with disabilities—you’re failing your organization by excluding a whole segment of potential talent. You are also opening up your organization to EEOC investigations. Accommodations should never be an afterthought; they should be an integral part of your comprehensive talent acquisition process. Offer accommodations to all candidates, not just those who proactively identify as having a disability.
Also, be prepared to offer accommodations before they are requested. Another area where the EEOC loves to issue huge fines against companies is when an individual’s candidacy is dropped because requested accommodations cannot be arranged in time to consider them for the position they applied for. This is why it is so critical to have contracts in place for interpreters and CART.
Making your interview process accessible isn’t just about checking boxes for compliance; it’s about recognizing that diversity includes disability and that inclusion means making room for everyone at the table. Accommodations aren’t about lowering the bar—they’re about giving every candidate a fair chance to show what they can bring to your team.
An inclusive interview process doesn’t just benefit candidates with disabilities; it benefits everyone. It sends a message that your company values diversity and inclusion and is committed to creating an environment where everyone has the opportunity to succeed. This is especially important for younger candidates, who are vastly more likely to apply to companies they believe are inclusive. The next time you’re planning an interview, take a moment to think about accessibility.

item.title: Why don't we use black text anymore? That's an Excellent Question, Diana!
item.description: Sometimes it's a good thing I’m not in an office during work hours. Here’s a perfect example of why. When I saw the headline of one of my regular email subscriptions, I screamed out loud, Damn
item.content:encoded:
Sometimes it's a good thing I’m not in an office during work hours. Here’s a perfect example of why. When I saw the headline of one of my regular email subscriptions, I screamed out loud, _Damn skippy! I’ve been asking that question for years_!
What was the headline that elicited such an enthusiastic response? The headline read: [_Why don't we use black text anymore_](https://a11ywithdiana.substack.com/p/why-dont-we-use-black-text-anymore? "This link leaves the DubBlog website.")_?_ It was pinned by [Diana Khalipina](https://www.linkedin.com/in/diana-khalipina/ "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") [](https://www.linkedin.com/in/diana-khalipina/ "This link leaves the DubBlog website.")(LinkedIn) in the Sept.6 issue of her daily publication titled [_A11y explained with Diana_](https://a11ywithdiana.substack.com/p/why-dont-we-use-black-text-anymore? "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") [](https://a11ywithdiana.substack.com/p/why-dont-we-use-black-text-anymore? "This link leaves the DubBlog website.")(Substack)
After [reading her post](https://a11ywithdiana.substack.com/p/why-dont-we-use-black-text-anymore? "This link leaves the DubBlog website."), I was even more convinced. Gray text has its place, but it's time to bring black text back.
As web design moved toward minimalist layouts in the 2010s, designers increasingly used shades of gray instead of black for body copy, labels, metadata, and supporting content. The idea was simple. Black text looked too heavy, while gray created a softer, cleaner visual hierarchy and made body copy feel less visually dominant.
The problem is that **subtle** for some can mean **harder to read** for others.
The concern isn't that gray is inherently inaccessible. It's how much contrast it has against its background. Gray text on a white background can look elegant on a large monitor in a controlled environment. Still, it can become surprisingly difficult to read for someone with low vision or [reduced contrast sensitivity](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/medgen/1671089 "This link leaves the DubBlog website.").
And the difficulties are not limited to people who identify as having a visual disability.
Try reading light-gray text on your phone outdoors. Add sunlight, screen glare, a smaller display, or a slightly older pair of eyes. Suddenly, that carefully chosen **subtle** gray isn't so elegant. It’s simply difficult to see.
Black or near-black text generally provides the strongest contrast on white backgrounds, making body copy easier to read, especially for people with low vision or in bright, glare-heavy conditions. Gray text can work for secondary content, but lighter shades may be harder to perceive and can fall below WCAG contrast requirements.
WCAG 2.2 Level AA requires a [4.5:1 contrast ratio](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/contrast-minimum.html "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") for normal-sized text and 3:1 for large text. And according to WebAIM,
> _You cannot round a contrast ratio up to 4.5:1. For example, #777777, a commonly-used shade of gray with a 4.47:1 contrast ratio, does not meet this requirement. ~ [Contrast and Color Accessibility](https://webaim.org/articles/contrast/ "This link leaves the DubBlog website.")_
This is #777777 gray text on a white background.
When in doubt, choose darker text to maximize readability and move closer to meeting accessibility requirements.
Black or near-black text doesn't have to mean abandoning visual hierarchy. Use font size, weight, spacing, layout, and white space to [make visual design more accessible to people with disabilities](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tips/designing/ "This link leaves the DubBlog website."). Gray still has its place. But if we're choosing between **subtle** and **readable**, perhaps readable should win more often. Good design shouldn't ask users to work harder to read the content.
It isn't about making every website look like a newspaper. It's about giving the words enough visual weight to hold up in real-world conditions. A very dark gray can provide plenty of contrast while feeling slightly softer than pure black. The key is to check the contrast and test it under different lighting conditions rather than simply eyeballing whether a color is accessible.
Accessibility isn't just about whether something technically passes a test. It's about whether people can comfortably use it in the real world.
If black text gives your readers a better experience, why wouldn't you use it?
## Resources
- [Understanding WCAG 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum)](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/contrast-minimum.html "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") - [WebAIM: Contrast and Color Accessibility](https://webaim.org/articles/contrast/ "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") - [WebAIM Contrast Checker](https://webaim.org/resources/contrastchecker/ "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") - [Low-Contrast Text Is Not the Answer](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/low-contrast/ "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") - [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") - [Specifying text and background colors of secondary content such as banners, features and navigation in CSS while not specifying text and background colors of the main content](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Techniques/css/C23 "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") (W3C Technique)

item.title: How Much ALT Text is Too Much ALT Text?
item.description: While scrolling through LinkedIn the other day, I came across a post from a former intern from my higher-education days. He was sharing a website redesign project he had worked on, and I was excited
item.content:encoded:
While scrolling through LinkedIn the other day, I came across a post from a former intern from my higher-education days. He was sharing a website redesign project he had worked on, and I was excited to see what he’d created. Naturally, I checked out the website and, of course, ran the WAVE extension to see if he remembered what I’d taught him about accessibility.😉
To my delight, he had incorporated accessibility best practices throughout the new site. (Caveat: As much as he could, given the web design tool he was working with.)
But something caught my eye. Not anything he had neglected, but an error description. WAVE had flagged several images, giving this reason: _An image has very long alternative text._
_![WAVE screen with a red circle highlighting the error message.](../../images/blog-content/2026/image-has-long-alt.png)_
I quickly inspected one of the images and found the ALT text: _Orchestra performers playing string and wind instruments during a concert, dressed formally in tuxedos and black dresses._
_![Code view in WAVE with the ALT text highlighted with a green box.](../../images/blog-content/2026/long-alt-in-code.png)_
Turns out that's a surprisingly common flag and a useful one, because _long ALT text_ isn't really about length. It's about intent. And that flag points to something screen reader users have to deal with directly.
## How Long is Too Long?
There is no _official_ character limit for ALT text, at least not one I can find. Even WCAG doesn’t set a hard number.
Still, it's worth taking seriously, because long ALT text usually signals one of two things: either the ALT text is repeating content already visible on the webpage, or it's trying to do a job the ALT attribute was never meant to do.
Most guidance converges on a similar range: roughly one sentence, often cited as 100 - 150 characters.
WebAIM's own [guide to alternative text](https://webaim.org/techniques/alttext/) is clear: ALT text should be equivalent and succinct, and it shouldn't duplicate what's already presented in nearby text or captions.
The W3C's [Web Accessibility Initiative](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/tips/) says much the same: ALT text should be the most concise description possible, and once you need more than a short phrase or sentence, a [long-description technique](https://dubbot.com/dubblog/2023/describing-images.html) is the better tool than trying to include **everything** in the ALT text.
## Why Does Too Much ALT Text Matter?
Length matters because of how assistive technology delivers that text. Remember, ALT text has no internal structure, no formatting, no headings, no way to jump by sentence or word the way a screen reader moves through webpage content. Some screen readers cope with very long ALT text by breaking it into chunks and announcing each one separately, so a single image can sound like several unrelated items.
In addition, symbols and line breaks can be skipped or garbled, and an embedded URL is often read aloud letter by letter instead of treated as a link.
A sighted visitor can scan a busy image pretty quickly. A screen reader user has to hear the whole thing, in order, every time. There is no equivalent shortcut.
That's the _real cost_ of long ALT text, not a failed check. Again, it’s about intent. It shapes the listening experience for the very person ALT text is meant to serve.
I don’t see these flagged images as a gotcha moment for my former intern. If anything, they were the perfect full-circle teaching moment. Because even a website built with accessibility in mind from day one can have a few gray areas. Showing us, once again, the critical roles of [context awareness and human oversight](https://dubbot.com/dubblog/2026/the-role-of-context-awareness-in-manual-accessibility-testing.html) in accessibility testing.
## Resources
- [Long ALT](https://adrianroselli.com/2024/04/long-alt.html) - [WebAIM: ALTernative Text](https://webaim.org/techniques/alttext/) - [W3C WAI: Images Tutorial — Tips](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/tips/) - [WAVE Alert Rule Set — UMN Duluth ITSS](https://www.d.umn.edu/itss/training/online/manual_testing/alert_ruleset.html)

item.title: Dark Mode vs. Light Mode: Preference, Trend, or an Accessibility Question?
item.description: Dark mode is no longer a niche developer preference. With the 2019-2020 releases of iOS 13, Android 10, and Windows / macOS system-level toggles into the mainstream, dark mode has since become a
item.content:encoded:
Dark mode is no longer a niche developer preference. With the 2019-2020 releases of iOS 13, Android 10, and Windows / macOS system-level toggles into the mainstream, dark mode has since become a widely offered option.
Last week, the Support Team received an unusual support issue related to dark mode. That conversation later led to a discussion with the whole team comparing dark vs. light mode preferences and why.
As the conversation unfolded on Slack, it was clear that, based on who responded, most DubBot team members are fans of dark mode and use it regularly.
Their reasons were mostly physical, such as tired eyes, light sensitivity, and screen fatigue by the end of the day. Some teammates run dark mode permanently and layer on extra tools like blue-light glasses, auto-dimming lenses, and even e-ink readers. Others fine-tune the iOS [Reduce White Point](https://applemagazine.com/ios-reduce-white-point/ "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") setting and make it a shortcut. A few, including me, actually prefer bright screens and find dark interfaces harder to read.
That mix is probably a fair representation of users in general and a pretty good reminder that accessibility isn't always about finding one setting that's best for everyone.
A design that feels comfortable to one person can be difficult or unpleasant for another.
## User Preference Matters
### Dark Mode Isn't Automatically More Accessible
It's easy to think of dark mode as strictly an accessibility feature. And for some users, it absolutely can improve the experience.
But dark mode itself doesn't guarantee an accessible interface. Accessibility fundamentals must be baked in. Sufficient contrast is essential throughout the interface, not just for text and backgrounds. Keyboard users need visible focus indicators regardless of theme, and non-text elements like buttons, form controls, and graphics need adequate contrast as well. Interactive states like hover, focus, active, selected, and disabled should stay distinguishable, and components should remain equally identifiable and usable across theme changes. Images and graphics also deserve attention, since one that works well on a light background won't necessarily work on a dark one.
And then there’s this: **a page can pass accessibility checks in one mode and fail them in another.** This was actually the issue that sparked our conversation.
### Light Mode and Dark Mode Can Create Different Accessibility Issues
Imagine a website where dark mode passes automated contrast testing, but light mode uncovers several contrast failures.
A text color that has enough contrast in dark mode may not have enough contrast in light mode. A border color that works with one background may disappear against another. A focus indicator that is highly visible in dark mode may become nearly invisible in light mode.
And then there are user preferences, variables like ones mentioned in our conversation. Folks mentioned using things like Reduce White Point, blue-light-filtering glasses, automatic dark mode, and even specialized displays designed to reduce screen glare and brightness.
These are not necessarily accessibility tools, but they are examples of how people customize their digital environments to make screens more comfortable and easier to use.
When designing dark and light modes, the goal should be to make sure **both experiences are accessible, usable, and visually effective**.
To help make that happen, keep a few things in mind:
- **Give users a choice when appropriate -** If your interface supports both light and dark modes, let users choose the experience that works best for them.
- **Respect system settings -** Many users have already chosen a preferred theme at the operating-system level. Your website should respect that preference rather than making users override it.
- **Test every supported version -** Run accessibility checks on both light and dark themes. Passing one version doesn't guarantee the other will pass.
- **Look beyond contrast -** Color contrast matters, but it’s only one aspect of accessibility. Check focus indicators, component states, icons, borders, images, and other visual cues in both themes.
## The Real Preference Isn't Light vs. Dark
The team conversation started out by just learning which mode folks prefer. It ended up an excellent illustration of why accessibility is rarely that simple.
Some people want dark mode all the time. Some want it only at night. Some prefer light mode. Some people adjust their devices in other ways to make screens easier to use.
No single setting solves everyone's needs. And that's okay.
The goal of accessible design isn't to pick the universally correct color scheme. It's to create experiences that _respect the fact that different people need different things_.
Accessibility rarely comes down to one setting that works for everyone. And sometimes, the best accessibility feature is simply having a choice.
## Resources
- [12 Principles & Best Practices of Dark Mode Design](https://uxcel.com/blog/12-principles-of-dark-mode-design-627 "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") - [StatCounter — Android Version Market Share Worldwide](https://gs.statcounter.com/android-version-market-share/mobile-tablet/worldwide "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") (July 2026 snapshot) - [StatCounter — iOS Version Market Share Worldwide](https://gs.statcounter.com/ios-version-market-share/mobile-tablet/worldwide "This link leaves the DubBlog website.") (July 2026 snapshot) - [A Brief History of Dark Mode - From the Matrix-like Displays of the Early ’80s to Today](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/a-brief-history-of-dark-mode-from-the-matrix-like-displays-of-the-early-80s-to-today/#:~:text=Nascent%20CRT%20technology%20wasn%27t,screens%2C%20dark%20mode%20was%20default. "This link leaves the DubBlog website.")
A human author creates the DubBlog posts. The AI tools Gemini and ChatGPT are sometimes used to brainstorm subject ideas, generate blog post outlines, and rephrase specific sections of content. Our marketing team carefully reviews all final drafts for accuracy and authenticity. The opinions and perspectives expressed remain the sole responsibility of the human author.
